summary:
The picture of you, Isa, is sensational. I am so proud to have a daughter that looks like that! And I’m equally proud of you, Nancy, for bringing her up to such a level of beauty and vitality. Wow. Thank you so much. We’ll have a few pictures of the baby to send you in a week or so. 

Nancy, you will be receiving two hundred dollars from me very soon—as soon as the D.A.’s office sends me the computer form which I have to enclose. I’ve already bought the two $100 checks for you. They’ll surely arrive before Christmas. But I have to wait on the D.A.’s letter and form to me; if I could send them to you direct they’d be in this letter right now. So just hang on. His letter generally gets here the fifth or sixth of the month; it may arrive tomorrow, and I’ll send the checks up airmail pronto. Your letter, Nancy, is the letter of a sane person with great insight and vast courage. You may have been sick once—but so was I—and so was Annie—we all were in the funny farm, were we not, along with lots of other people ... but there’s nothing sick about your letter. I guarantee you that happiness and salva­ tion are absolutely possible for you, and I would guess are setting in already. No, you’re not a nut. I feel that way about myself every now and then ... within the last three months I’ve tried again and again to enter the LeHabre psychiatric Hos­ pital—it’s been touch and go.
